utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The solemn declaration to speak the truth, which you made at the outset of your evidence continues to apply to the evidence today. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are you rested?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are there any examples of Serbs moving out and even leaving their property to Siptars?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are numerous examples of that, because that's how it was in those wartime conditions. People helped each other and tried to make due any way they could. And here's an example. There was a well-known professor of mathematics from Pristina university, Toma Milenkovic. Immediately after the air-strikes began, he moved away. And he had a good neighbour, Semsudin Hejdija [phoen] and his son Halil. And Semsudin had four sons. He gave them the keys to his flat and he gave them his fridge, because his neighbour had a cevapcici restaurant, and he said that he could use his fridge. That's an example for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You mentioned migration in Pristina, moving out. Could you please tell me when this peaked.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, moving of the population out of Pristina began --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It grew in intensity especially after the air-strikes of the very centre of town, which was on the 7th of April. After that, this migration increased, especially because some crucial facilities, such as the transformer station in Pristina were bombed. The waterworks near Badovac supplying Pristina with water were also bombed. Communications were damaged. People were in a panic because telephone lines had been cut off. Only some telephone lines were established using an old switchboard, a makeshift switchboard, and only some people had access to phone lines. So after that, this movement increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You're a witness of the events in Pristina. Can you tell me the targeted facilities in Pristina and the surroundings, what was the relationship between civilian and military facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately 90 per cent to 10 per cent. 90 per cent of the targets hit in Pristina were civilian targets. The only military target in Pristina was the Pristina barracks. That was bombed, but the barracks had been abandoned because the 15th Armoured Brigade had left the barracks before the aggression and taken up their positions, and the remaining positions were all civilian positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, did you see columns of civilians in the town of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did see columns of civilians moving through the town of Pristina. I would see them in the immediate vicinity of my command post, some 10 metres away from where my command post was. They often passed by there in the course of the aggression, in both directions. These columns moved from several directions, especially from the direction of Donje Ljubce, Grastica, via Vranjevac, passing by the municipal court and the municipal building, then along Mladina Popovica Street, passing by the secondary school and the Proleterske Street; and then it would go down -- part of it will go down Vidovdanska Street, and another part through Belgradska Street. And then after a while, the same columns would go back, the same people would be in those columns. The aim, especially in the area from Ljubce to Grastica was to have terrorists join those columns who threw away their weapons and fled before the forces fighting them and shooting at them. That's it in brief. It was an imitation of migration, similar to what happened in 1990, when they pretended to be poisoned by non-existent poisons, and that's a well-known incident that I don't want to dwell on any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am unclear, you should know, Mr. Cepic, about how you know whether a column is leaving because of the bombing or is leaving as some device organised by the KLA. It's very vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We'll try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the columns you described as moving through Pristina, did you recognize the same people in those columns sometimes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the columns that moved through Pristina, especially those that passed by the building where my command was, after they passed in one direction, I would see the same people - not just I, but other members of my command - would see the same people going back in the other direction, along the same route. We even asked some of them where they were going, and they would say, "We don't know. That's what they told us. That's what they told us to do." I was born there. I had lived there for a long time. I knew a lot of people personally. And that's why I was able to recognize them and know that they were the very same people moving first in one direction and then back in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these different columns from the ones that were migrating to escape the bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer is as follows: Some of those columns behaved in the way I have just described. Some citizens really fled to escape the bombs. They were concerned and frightened of the bombing. Some had had relatives killed or wounded by the bombs. And these were civilians fleeing. However, there were many of those that I've just described who were simply pretending to migrate, and these were more numerous than the former category. At least, as far as the town of Pristina is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, in the streets of Pristina, did you see prominent Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw many Albanians. I socialised with some of them at my command post, because it was located in the municipal building and they came to work there every day, and I would also see some well-known Albanians walking down the street. For example, the notorious ideologue of the terrorists, Adem Demaci. He would pass by my command almost every day. He wore a beige coat, nearly white. It was very light in colour. And he would pass by without hindrance, first in one direction and then the other, throughout the entire aggression. I noticed him, and so did other members of my command. And this also relates to others. But, well, this is just an example. And this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify a point, what is Adem Demaci known for? Why is he notorious?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is notorious because of many bad things. Many years before, he had been sentenced for terrorist activity. Some 30 years before, he had been sentenced to nine years for terrorist activity. That was his first sentence. And my father was a juror in that trial. Later on, he was sentenced to 13 years again. He spent a large part of his life in prison for inciting terrorism and for terrorism. That's it in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And are these judgements from the SFRY period?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They date from the '60s, after the fourth plenum.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, what were the living conditions in the town of Pristina itself?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, in the town of Pristina, in view of the daily bombing and the wartime conditions, in line with these conditions -- or rather, if we take these conditions into account, life went on more or less as normal, speaking in relative terms. For example, all the bakeries in town were operating. The privately-owned bakeries, owned both by Siptars and Serbs, continued operating, as did a large state-owned bakery. The television institutions continued operating in four languages: Siptar, Serb, Roma, and a fourth one. Newspapers were published and distributed, including newspapers in the Siptar language. Shops were open. The clinical hospital centre treated all citizens. The maternity ward was operating. And as I frequently had contacts with the State Registry Office - the chief of that service was Adnan - I remember more than 100 Siptar children were inscribed in the register of births. They were born in Pristina Hospital; although, many children were not entered into the registers because of the war. But all institutions were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 6, 17. I believe the witness said a Turkish language as well and he said the radio was operating in all four languages as well. It hasn't been entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, during the aggression, were old-age pensions paid to citizens regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This function of local self-management also continued to operate. When the post office, the main post office in Pristina was hit, then it was no longer possible to use postal services and to pay out old-age pensions. The post office immediately responded and set up makeshift desks in the Union Building next to the theatre, which was across the road from the post office. There was more than one desk operating, and people queued up at these desks to get their old-age pensions. And most of these were Siptars. Of course, because there were more of them living in the town and receiving old-age pensions. And the same applied to Gracanica, one of the largest places in Pristina municipality. Old-age pensions for the villages of Ajvalija, Mramor, Slivovo, Dragovac, Saskovac, and all the surroundings villages were also paid out. That's as far as old-age pensions are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you remember any names of people queueing up to get their pension -- pensions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, pensions were paid to all citizens inter alia because the pension fund had a republican pension fund and also a military pension fund. I recognized many of those who were military pensioners getting their pensions there. I won't enumerate them now, but there were many of them, and many among them would stay there, leave Kosovo, and come back again several times during the aggression. They would move away and then they would come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the bakery as operating throughout the war. Do you know what the ratio of employees in the bakery was, as far as ethnic affiliation goes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the city bakery, the main one, on the road leading to Kosovo Polje, the director was Djordje Simic, produced about 20 to 25 thousand kilogrammes of bread per day, which was similar to the production before the aggression. The breakdown of employees was as follows: More than two-thirds were Siptars, especially in direct production, because production of bread in Kosovo is not in the Serb tradition. But even without that many work organisations, many enterprises introduced work obligation, and in socially owned institutions and other enterprises, more than 50 per cent were Siptars, and they continued to come to work regularly. Even the investigating court had Siptar employees, and they came to work and participated in investigations, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's talk now about houses of worship and religious buildings. Were any such buildings in the town of Pristina damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the city of Pristina, I can say that not a single house of worship or religious building was either damaged or destroyed. I am referring to Islamic, Catholic, and Orthodox buildings. And I'm especially referring to Islamic ones. In the vicinity of my command, there were two very important and large mosques which represent the cultural heritage of Islam, the Carska or Emperor's Mosque, Jasar Pasa's Mosque, and a third mosque, and they all remained undamaged, as did the other facilities during the aggression, religious services were held there. I saw that personally. But as regards Orthodox buildings, the situation was not the same. The Orthodox cemetery in Pristina was bombed more than once, and on one occasion it was bombed when I was there, because I was attending a funeral, the funeral of an officer who had been killed. His name was Milic. He had a twin brother who was -- and he was killed in the NATO bombing. And we barely managed to complete the funeral. We were almost all killed, and many graves were damaged. In the vicinity of Pristina, the cemetery in Gornja Brnjica was damaged, as was the cemetery church, part of the cultural heritage and monument to the Kosovo battle at Gazimestan were also damaged, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regardless of whether house of worship belonged to the Catholic, Orthodox, or Muslim faith, were any military facilities or equipment placed in any one of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I categorically state that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard about the town of Pristina, but let's talk about the surrounding villages now -- or actually, before that, I'm interested in the following: Did cluster bombs hit Pristina and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Pristina and in the surrounding area, there were many hits by cluster bombs. Some of the remains of these cluster bombs were collected by us, and out of these remains we made a small exhibition in front of our command. So all citizens, Serbs, Siptars, and all passers-by could see this collection of those remains. This was even filmed by some foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just give me an example of the largest villages around Pristina. What was life like? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll enumerate a few villages, although Pristina as a municipality includes over 46 villages. I'm going to mention those that are the closest and that are the most characteristic. For example, the village of Gracanica is the largest village inhabited by Serbs. That goes for the entire Kosovo and Metohija. Life was relatively normal there, except for the fact that very close to the monastery of Gracanica and the village of Gracanica, there were many bombings of military facilities; namely, a warehouse that was nearby. So this disturbed the citizens. Otherwise, life went on as normal. And let me say that in the village there was a big bakery that was operating, that worked before the war too. A Siptar, Leki Nikolj [phoen] was the owner of that factory. He baked bread there, and he sold his bread to citizens during the aggression, before the aggression, after the aggression. When his son got killed, the citizens of Gracanica, Serbs, went to the funeral of his son, to his native village in Metohija. So there's that example. Then there's also the village of Ajvalija that was one of the larger Siptar villages before the aggression. Although, before that it had mostly been populated by Serbs. Life in that village evolved in a rather organized way. There are many examples of Serbs helping each other out, Serb and Siptars actually helping each other out with food supplies and so on; Serbs were very few there actually. All shops were open. All the shops that were open were only owned by Siptars. Primarily the families of Vitija, Gashi, Berisha, those shops were open on a regular basis. The mosque --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Not all of this can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mosque in the village of Gracanica did not only remain undamaged but religious services were held regularly there. As a matter of fact, this village took in some Siptar refugees from the surrounding villages. The village council took them in. The village council included the families of Pacoli [phoen], Vitija, and Drela. An attempt was made to have the population moved out of this village on two occasions, actually, Siptars; namely, in the direction of Kolonija, Ajvalija, Vucji Potok, Mramor. The other direction was Vucji Potok and Mramor. That is where they had been promised to be taken in by the terrorist forces. The terrorist forces would organise their life there. Some of them went there and stayed there for a day or two, and then went back to their own village, realizing that that had not been true. And that is where they stayed, in their own village until the end of the aggression. They lived a peaceful life. No one was hurt, except for one citizen, Sopiani, who in the area of Mramor and Mranice, he was a victim and no one knows why. The village of Maticane, this is also one of the biggest villages, closest to the town of Pristina. It is inhabited by Siptars. There were about 20 houses of Serbs. Life in that village was also practically normal, except that in that village the few Serbs there during the aggression and just before the aggression, and later on during the aggression, they were expelled, and some were even killed and kidnapped. For example, Momir Kostic was kidnapped and his wife was killed. They were from that village. And the terrorists did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And many others, not to enumerate all the names now. A woman by the name of Julijana was killed. Her husband was killed. And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The village of Kisnica, actually, a mining town near the Gracanica Jezero. It's an old mine with a mining colony. It was inhabited both by Serbs and Siptars. That mine used to work very intensively. Before the aggression, there was a decline in its production and it worked a very small capacity. Also, some of its facilities worked throughout the aggression. Serbs and Siptars had work assignments throughout the aggression. And the command post of the corps command was there for a while. It happened that way. Irrespective of that, life went on as normal. The mining clinic was open as well. It was headed by a doctor, Dr. Jahija, an Albanian. He's a dentist, actually, and he was head of that clinic or infirmary. And nearby there was a refugee centre where refugees were put up, Serbs who had fled from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that centre during the course of the aggression, a number of Siptars who had fled from some other places near Pristina were put up. They were put up together with the Serb refugees, and they shared the same destiny. They were only about 100 metres away from the command post of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, my last question: The members of the Army of Yugoslavia in Pristina, did they participate in any way in expelling citizens?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a single example of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I'll have a few questions for you. You saw Defence Exhibit 5D348. Could we please see it on our screens. Just to speed things up. While we're waiting for this document, let me say -- ah, here it is. Could we just have paragraph 1 zoomed in on. As you can see, it says here: "After the planned relocation of the Pristina Command outside the building of the command." Now I want to ask you the following: Once the command of the Pristina Corps was relocated, did it ever go back during the course of the war? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the command was relocated, from this building that was its headquarters in peacetime and where I was too, the corps command never returned there. I, as garrison commander, took it upon myself to provide external security for it; however, inside the command was never there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. You have a great deal of experience in this. Could you please explain to us amateurs what this Pristina Corps Command looks like in peacetime, and generally speaking what it looks like. How many people are there? What happens there? What is required in order to command the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I, as a member of the command, can explain this briefly; although, that is not exactly my line of work in terms of my function, but I will tell you about it. The corps command especially and any command is a complex mechanism. It has several organisational parts, especially the corps command according to wartime establishment is deployed in a broad area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I asked you about peacetime. What was it like in peacetime? The command of the Pristina Corps while it was in that building.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While it was in that building, we, the entire peacetime command, that had about 100 men, was headquartered there. It wasn't only the command of the Pristina Corps that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How many storeys does this building have?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's five storeys. I may be making a mistake by one, but I think it's five storeys.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you took care of that building as you -- as you were appointed commander of the Pristina garrison, as it says here. I want to ask you the following: During the course of the war -- actually, let's do it this way: Did some people enter that building from the military? For example, General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, then some other people from the police, and then some civilians too; and then from that building, from that command post that was there in peacetime -- are you following me? The way you described it. Did these people command the units of the Army of Yugoslavia and MUP from there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. I categorically state that that was not the case, because the commander of the guard would have had to inform me about this. That was Vuckovic. But I would have known myself too.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One more question. In order -- in order to command, do you need some kind of communications? Do you need to keep up communications? Or does somebody just sit in a room and command through the window, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot command a modern war without modern communications equipment and systems of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there such systems during the course of the war in that building, the ones that you're talking about now?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you quite briefly. This is not exactly my line of work. But the 52nd Centre for Communications was there. However, when the aggressions started, the entire 52nd Stationary Centre for Communications was relocated there, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question: At the Grand Hotel, you said -- I'm just saying this for the transcript. You said that this 52nd -- answer: "Stationary centre of communications headed by Colonel Mladenovic relocated from that building at the beginning of the aggression."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. The transcript doesn't seem to be right again. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We better have that answer again. The question was: Were there such systems - that's modern communications equipment and systems - during the course of the war in that building? That is, the original Pristina Corps Command centre. What's the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer to that question is as follows: There weren't any people there who were working for them, and equipment was not there. If there had been such equipment, it was taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What -- your answer, though, was -- was quite different from that. It -- it had something to do with the 52nd Centre for Communications. What did you tell us about that? Because it's not been -- apparently not been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that centre, when the aggression started, was relocated from that place, moved out of that place, in accordance with a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Last question, Colonel. You mentioned some kind of information centre when you were speaking, of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned the information centre of the Pristina Corps. Could you please tell us, where was that centre located? In what building? And what purpose did it serve?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That information centre was located in the building of the Grand Hotel, and it mostly provided information to the public and also liaised with the media, informing the public about the developments in Kosovo and Metohija at that time, and in particular with the efforts of the army, to deal with the wartime conditions and to establish new -- a proper way of life for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that the Pristina Corps Command was not located at that hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was not headquartered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I take it I can refer to you as "Colonel"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yes. Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Before I -- before I start on a more substantive topic, I'd just like to go back to one thing you said yesterday in answer to my learned friend. Do you remember being asked about whether the VJ artillery would fire from Vranjevac to the village of Kojlovica? Do you remember a question about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your answer to that question was that it did not take place, and you said, and I quote: "Especially since Kojlovica is a mixed village, populated by both Serbs and Albanians." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. But it was in the context of the previous sentences, so it cannot just stand alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: I take it when you said "especially that it was a mixed village," you were saying that it's inconceivable that the VJ would fire upon Serb civilians. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it is inconceivable for the Army of Yugoslavia to open fire on any civilians. So as far as the Army of Yugoslavia was concerned, civilians both of Siptar ethnic background and Serbs, they were all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that that's if the village was solely populated by Albanian civilians, it would not make a difference.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said - and let me repeat once again - the Army of Yugoslavia never opened fire on any civilians, and it would never do that. It would be in contravention of the international conventions and customs of war, and also it would be contrary to our laws. All the soldiers and all the officers of the Army of Yugoslavia were aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you said that throughout the conflict, at least when NATO started its bombing campaign, you were in Pristina. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And during the period that the conflict continued, I take it you remained in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so you didn't have the opportunity to visit the other outer lying municipalities within Kosovo itself, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, I left Pristina; that was during the aggression. I asked the corps commander for permission, and he allowed me to leave and to visit my son in the Vitina area. I did that. I took one day off. I went there and I returned in the same day. I spent the remainder of the time in Pristina and in its vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, then. So in answer to my question, apart from that one day where you had a family visit, if I can put it that way, you did not visit the other command posts of the VJ throughout Kosovo and Metohija, did you, during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer to your question is as follows: In the town of Pristina, there were many other military units. These units had their own command posts. I visited some of those, such as on two or three occasions I visited the command post of the Pristina Military Department and the command post of the Military District of Pristina. I also visited -- but in fact, this was not just a visit. I went to the corps command. It was an official visit. That was in Kisnica. And this is all I can remember at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Perhaps -- perhaps my question was not precise enough. I just want you to confirm for me that during the conflict you were not -- you did not visit the military establishments in, for example, Pec or Prizren or Kosovo Polje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you must accept that you would not know whether the VJ in those areas - and of course, they -- they were present in those areas - you would not know whether they were in fact firing at civilians or violating international humanitarian law, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could not really say that I don't know about that, because you don't gain all your knowledge by seeing things for yourself; although, if you are an eyewitness, this is a much more certain kind of knowledge and it makes you a more reliable witness. I had many contacts with the troops, with the officers, and I never got any such information. That's number one. Number two, from the point of view of what we had been trained and taught to do and what we had prepared before the aggression, I was absolutely sure that nothing of the sort could actually happen. So that would be my answer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your job was to be the group commander of the Pristina garrison, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I led a command group that I described earlier, and the composition was also described, and the commander of the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in that group, were there departments that were actively involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this yesterday, and let me repeat today: In that group, there were no combat elements. And in the course of the aggression, up until the Kumanovo Agreement, we never participated in combat. None of the members of that group and of the garrison command fired a single bullet at anyone. In fact, nobody ever trained their weapons at anyone at all. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me ask you about that, actually. I remember yesterday -- in fact, you probably remember yourself -- that you were asked if -- if you and your colleagues ever fired a single bullet, and your answer was that you never even pointed a barrel at someone. You remember that answer?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. And I can say that this was in the period of the aggression, up until the signing of the Kumanovo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I take it that -- well, if you could just tell the Court, within the garrison and within the group that you commanded, how many soldiers were there, roughly? Soldiers, officers. Can you give us a number, please.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the strength changed from time to time, and it increased in relation to the initial period, but it was between 100 and 150 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you yourself and, indeed, the other officers were armed during the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of us in this group were armed. We had the kind of weapons envisaged by the establishment, so not just any weapons we wanted but weapons that were issued in accordance with the peacetime and wartime establishment. That would be mostly rifles and pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did any of your officers or did yourself, did you have semiautomatic rifles, for example, Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had M-70A rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you would agree with me that your garrison and you yourself and your fellow soldiers would have been legitimate military targets. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you whether we were a legitimate military target. I feel no need to discuss this topic at all. I carried out my duties. I don't know if I was a target of any kind. At that time, it really didn't interest me. I had my tasks and I focused on carrying them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, for someone such as yourself, who has had considerable experience in the army, I take it you know whether -- or I take it you know what a legitimate military target is.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. Okay. Let's say that I knew that I was a legitimate military target, but not a target for terrorists. War had been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let's just stick to the time period when war started. By the same token - and we've had evidence in this trial that the VJ were in conflict with an armed rebellion, or the KLA. You know that existed, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia was not in conflict with the terrorist forces. That is not true. The terrorist forces were in conflict with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let's just say that there happened to be -- irrespective of who started a particular action, you would agree with me that the VJ were entitled to fire and to neutralise members of the KLA. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia was entitled, pursuant to the Constitution and the Law on the Army and the Rules of Service. So its personnel was entitled to open fire not only on terrorists, on Siptar terrorists, but also on everybody else who may have attacked it and fired on it. So any other parties -- had any other parties attacked the army or its personnel, they would get the same response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so during certain battles or in the conflict between the VJ and the KLA, you would agree with me that it would be to the VJ's advantage if they were to neutralise a KLA terrorist or a -- a KLA company or a battalion. That would be to the VJ's advantage. Would you agree with that? In -- in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would not be in the army's favour if you have a broad look. It would be in favour of the people living there in that area, the people who suffered casualties because of the terrorist attacks. Siptars and Serbs alike. Because a terrorist, as you know all too well, killed many Siptars, and also many innocent Serbs. So it would favour the population, and the army would come last in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let's try and -- let's try and reach this point in another way. Let's -- let's take an hypothetical situation. You have two armies, two belligerents fighting a war. Are you with me on this at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can follow you, and I'm following you very carefully, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree that the purpose of each of those armies is to defeat their opposite or their enemies. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree with you partially. I will not agree with you when you say that these are two armies, because this is not true. These were not two armies. There was the Army of Yugoslavia and the Siptar terrorists on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I was actually giving you a hypothetical situation, so let's just stick with two -- two belligerents, two parties fighting against each other. And in that situation, you would agree with me that if one party has the opportunity to take out another member of that -- of their enemy party, then it would be something that would be done and something that would be advantageous to -- to the party firing the shot. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. You said a lot of things here, and I have really followed you very closely, and I don't know what the question is. You actually asked me several questions. I can answer each of them in turn, if that's what you want me to do. First of all, these are not two sides participating in combat, because one side is not participating in combat at all, and that would be the Army of Yugoslavia. You have combat if you have simultaneous attacks. Yet the army is not participating in this sense. It -- it is attacked by the terrorists, and then it responds, using appropriate assets, to those terrorist attacks. So this is something quite different to what you are trying to put to me in your question. I -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, we don't have the luxury of the time here for a theoretical debate about the rights and wrongs of the means of conflict between parties, the definition of their respective status, depending on whether they're terrorists, freedom fighters, or a -- a military organisation. And we found, I think, in general here that hypothetical questions are not well received by the witnesses who appear before us. They are generally suspicious of them and prefer to deal with the facts of the situation. So I wonder if you could concentrate more on dealing with questions that deal with the facts that this witness can perhaps assist us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm guided. I was actually trying to get to my eventual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, you told the Court that you yourself and your fellow soldiers never fired a shot.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I didn't say "never." I just said "in the course of the aggression." Up to the Kumanovo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also told the Court that during the conflict, there were KLA establishments within Pristina, and you spoke about terrorist attacks in Pristina. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You gave evidence yesterday that there were KLA formations in the area of Pristina and that there were allegedly terrorist attacks in Pristina. You remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is it really your evidence, Colonel, that you and your other 100 soldiers that were armed never fired a shot at these KLA terrorists in Pristina? Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm trying to tell the Court is what I want to tell the Court, and what I'm trying to say is that up to the Kumanovo Agreement, not a single member of the Kumanovo garrison [as interpreted] fired a single bullet. This is the third or fourth time I've been repeating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The term "Kumanovo garrison" has appeared in the transcript. Was that the name of your garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. What I was saying: Up to the Kumanovo Agreement, that is, the 10th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate entirely. And that also appears in the transcript. But it goes on to say: "Not a single member of the Kumanovo garrison fired a single bullet." I take it that wasn't a name given to the Pristina garrison that you were in temporary command of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's an error, an evident error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... For the transcript. Thank you very much. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So what I understand is that from the onset of the conflict, when NATO started its campaign, up until the 9th or 10th of June, in 1999, you and your fellow soldiers never fired a single shot at KLA groups within Pristina. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My evidence is that from the beginning of the NATO aggression, not campaign, and air-strikes, up until the Kumanovo Agreement, not a single member of the command of the garrison and the group I was in command of fired a single bullet at anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you also told us yesterday that there were almost daily attacks -- terrorist attacks in Pristina before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you also saying that none of your garrison fired shots in connection with these attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as you were able to see, Your Honour, I became the garrison commander as of the 30th of March. The aggression began on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can't speak to the earlier period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can, but in a different context, because I was not the garrison commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please -- please don't -- please don't try to mess us about, Mr. Filipovic. The question is about your personal knowledge of the use of weapons prior to the 23rd of March. Now, forget your exact status. What is your evidence about the use of weapons by members of that garrison in connection with KLA attacks prior to the commencement of the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the NATO aggression began, there were numerous attacks, both on civilians and on members of the army in the general area of Pristina. For example, on the 15th of March, there was an attack near Vranjevac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, deal with the question. Tell me whether or not the garrison fired shots in connection with any attack at all. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware that anyone fired from the garrison. I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It's straightforward. I don't need any more detail. If I want more detail, I'll ask for it. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So with the KLA that were in the town and these KLA groups, what in fact did the army do with respect to these groups?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrorist groups in the general area of Pristina launched attacks both on citizens and on members of the army in the general area. In the town itself, I did not see a single terrorist carrying terrorist insignia of any sort. They may have been terrorists, but we were unable to recognize them in the town, because terrorists are terrorists, according to what they do. But they did not wear any insignia in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, your evidence yesterday was that there were daily attacks by terrorists in Pristina before the aggression. You were able to tell us yesterday that terrorists were attacking. What Mr. Sachdeva wants to hear is what the army did about it. Can you not tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, nothing. For example, in March, two policemen were killed in the Pristina neighbourhood of Imsirovo. Four policemen were killed in the centre of Pristina. One was of Siptar ethnicity, and he was wounded. And the army did nothing, because it was not tasked with doing anything about that in town. It was other structures that responded, but there was nothing they could do because the terrorists were wearing civilian clothes and they fled the scene of the crime. And there are many other similar examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, I just want to talk to you briefly about your -- your role in the garrison. I understand that you were in charge of matters relating to housing and -- and personnel. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, my duty as the garrison commander is prescribed in the Rules of Service of the Army of Yugoslavia. My duties are prescribed for peacetime, and as a provision, in the Rules of Service, saying that in wartime all the duties remain the same. I hope you have a copy of these rules, and there you can see all the tasks. I can remember and enumerate many of them, but I may not be able to do so in the exact order that they're listed in the Rules of Service. If you need me to tell you, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, I think my question was relatively simple, but let me just ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again, experience tells us here that it is very unwise to ask a question which has clearly been answered in a straightforward way in the evidence in chief just to set the scene. It doesn't work. So it's much better to get straight to the issue that you want to ask about, and then you can go back and clarify the sort of formal part, if it turns out to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm guided, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, the information with respect to the strength of the Pristina Corps, in terms of personnel, I take it that you would regularly brief or at least brief the commander, General -- General Lazarevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you would do this at these meetings that you spoke about, the collegium meetings, and also the meetings that you had within the Pristina Corps during the conflict. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall all those meetings in detail, but I remember many things. I informed him of everything that was of interest. I did not keep quiet about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: With respect to the strength of the Pristina Corps in terms of personnel and manpower, if General Lazarevic sought information, you would be the person, you would be that point person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I'll tell you why. Because I was assistant commander for personnel affairs. It was my task to inform him of professional members. With respect to soldiers and conscripts, that was done by another department, which was called Department for Mobilisation and Replenishment, and it was Lieutenant-Colonel Simovic was at the head of that. I had other information also, but my primary task was professional members, which means officers, non-commissioned officers, and contract soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But in addition to those groups, you would also know the -- the amount of nonprofessional officers and -- and other such volunteers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for Prosecution Exhibit 2004 to be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a document from the Pristina Corps Command dated the 13th of April, 1999. And you'll see it's a report, a very urgent report to the 3rd Army and the Supreme Staff Command. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it has various subsections. And if I could ask you to go -- if I could ask to go to page 2 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. And you'll see, General -- Colonel, at the bottom part of the document you will see a section entitled "Effective manning level." Do you see that there? It's under section 3.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you will see under 3.1 that it is reported to the 3rd Army and to the Supreme Command Staff that the corps - and that is, I suggest, the Pristina Corps - is manned by 61.892 men. Do you see that written there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see further along that section that this figure is broken down into subcategories; namely, the amount of officers, the amount of non-commissioned officers, regular soldiers, and volunteers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that this means that the Pristina Corps had, in terms of military personnel, had almost 62.000 men. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, with reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And does that figure in this document, does that, with respect to your role within the Pristina Corps, does that figure appear to you to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to understand this better, the Pristina Corps, in terms of war establishment, had 30 to 34 thousand members in total. This figure here relates to the Pristina Corps with re-subordinated units. The corps itself in the wartime establishment had between 30 and 35 thousand members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, you'll see it that says 54.106 soldiers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And those soldiers -- those soldiers are within the Pristina Corps, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that also -- no, those soldiers were in the Pristina Corps with the re-subordinated units. That would be the correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, you don't see anything here about re-subordination, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not mentioned here, but it's implied.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it is reported by General Lazarevic to the 3rd Army and the Supreme Command Staff that the Pristina Corps has 62.000 -- roughly 62.000 soldiers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please see the signature, if that's possible, at the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, we can go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when this witness was asked to establish the authenticity of another document by the same organ, I was not allowed to do that, as it was not within the witness's sphere of competence. That was the 3rd combat report of the Pristina Corps. And I think the number of the exhibit was ... If you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was you trying to set the document up, was it not? In this instance, Mr. Filipovic sounds suspicious of the document and wants to see whether it's authentic. The situation is different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want so much to see whether it was authentic as to see who compiled it, because this document was compiled by the organ for recruitment and mobilisation, not the one headed by me. That was the organ headed by Lieutenant-Colonel Simovic. That was the reason I wanted to see what the initials were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, would you agree with me, though, that this is a report to the 3rd Army and to the Supreme Command Staff about the effective manpower of the Pristina Corps, irrespective of whether units have been subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that from the heading, to whom it's addressed and by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it that you agree with my question.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when I asked you earlier about this figure of 61.892 men, you mentioned reinforcements. What do you mean by "reinforcements"?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I basically abide by that. These are figures expressing the numbers of the Pristina Corps with the attached units, and these are the following units: First of all, the units of the Pristina Military District, the units of the 202nd Rear Base or logistics base, and some other smaller units. These units and the war composition of the Pristina Corps make up the numbers that can be seen in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go to Exhibit 5D00348, please. Colonel, this is the exhibit that you -- you commented upon in examination-in-chief, where it details your role and the role of the garrison. You remember this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in this document, it lists various departments that the garrison would comprise of. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: There is nothing in this document that suggests that matters related to procurement or supplies would be within the competence of the garrison. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with that, because this is an organisational document. It gives only the framework and the composition of that group as a whole; whereas, the tasks are formulated at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And not just that, but even before that. It's well known what their tasks are, because that's provided for in many previous documents. However, this document only deals with the organisation, what units will enter into this group, into its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you agree with me that in this document there is no mention of procurement or supplies.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. Many other jobs are not mentioned. Now one should mention whether the orchestra is to play or not and what they are doing? That would take us to extremes. This is an organisational document, and the tasks follow from other previous documents and tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what kind of document this is. I'm simply asking you to agree with me that there is no mention of procurement or supplies in this document. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but when you ask me like that, I cannot agree with you, because it doesn't say here that they should have three meals a day but we did have three meals a day. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, the question is very simple. You mustn't be suspicious of what complications might be created because you answer a simple question with a simple answer. You're being asked whether this document actually refers to procurement or supplies; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this document [Realtime transcript read in error "detention unit"] does not. The document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, earlier on in your testimony you spoke about -- I see my colleague is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe the -- the transcript says "detention unit" as I believe the witness says "document."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, earlier on in your testimony you spoke about the military court and the prosecutor's office. And we can see from this document that it is contained within the garrison. You remember answering a question about that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember speaking about the military prosecutor's office and the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also said that the work of the court and the prosecutor was independent and that you wouldn't have been privy to the substantive workings of that court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the work of the court and the work of the military prosecutor's office were independent in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that within your role in the garrison you weren't aware of the details of any cases that would have been submitted to the court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I was aware of some cases. For example, I was aware of a case because I was summoned to participate as a juror. It had to do with theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was that the only case you were aware of, because you were participating in it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lot of time has elapsed. I think that was the only case in which I played the role of a jury member. There may have been some others. I can't recall exactly. But I do know that the members of the garrison were very often summoned to participate as jury members in some cases before the military court of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I ask just one more question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. When cases --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Generally when cases were submitted to the court, in other words, the evidence, the documents, it wouldn't be -- as a matter of course, you wouldn't be reviewing those cases. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. I don't even know how many cases were filed before the court or what the outcome was. This information was not available to me, nor did I interfere in that, nor was that my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: We can take the break now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've departed from the issue of the procurement of supplies, have you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, actually not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, we need a break at this stage. That will be for 20 minutes. Could you leave the courtroom with the usher, please, and we'll see you again at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, I take it that during the -- during the conflict, during the war, you wouldn't know all the names of all the reserve officers that were attached to the Pristina Corps Command. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what my answer is: I knew all the officers of the command of the Pristina Corps. As for those who were assigned temporarily, I did not know all of them and I did not know all of their names. So, please, this is the category I'm talking about, temporarily assigned to work there. That is so, strictly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when you say you knew all the officers of the command of the Pristina Corps, I take it you would not know -- and you're answering my question in the affirmative -- you would not know all the names of all the reserve officers within that corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I certainly didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So then you would agree with the possibility -- that there is a possibility that the reserve officer called Tijanic, you may not have known whether that person existed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This is a question of the corps command. If we are talking about the corps command, that is something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We seem to have confused language here. The witness is quite clear that he knows the identity of all officers in the corps command except those temporarily assigned there, which is not necessarily a reserve officer. I don't know where the concept of reserve comes into this. That's quite distinct from claiming he knows everyone within the Pristina Corps. And it's important that you make that distinction when you're addressing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I thought I made the distinction with respect to the corps command, but let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. If you look at line 23 and 24, you'll see why the witness answered the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So would you know the names of all the reserve officers within the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't know -- well, as far as I know, the corps command, well, from this distance -- I don't really think that it had any reserve officers. I'm not quite certain of that, but I am more certain that the command of the corps did not have reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, assuming that they did, you wouldn't know the names of all the reserve officers. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this distance, I cannot give you a yes-or-no answer. Then, at that time, I knew everybody. And I was supposed to know everybody, at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Where was the procurement and supply department? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should have been in the logistics organ, the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the logistics organ was located where? Is that the 202nd logistics base?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. The logistics organ existed in the command of the Pristina Corps. The 202nd base is something separate. The corps command had its own logistics organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who was the head of the procurement and supplies section during the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the head, and I don't know whether that is exactly what it was called; however, Colonel Petkovic, Bratislav Petkovic, headed the logistics organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You don't know who was responsible for procurement and supplies within the corps command. Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know. These are internal organisational duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that if there was somebody called Tijanic that worked for the procurement and supplies section, you would not necessarily know that person. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since my organ dealt with personnel matters, all documents starting with dossiers ended up at my organ, so I knew all the first and last names from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Please tell the Court who was the head of the procurement and supplies section during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I don't know whether such an organ existed. There was a logistics organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said that you had meetings with members of the corps command on a -- on a regular basis, and you also attended collegium meetings. Just tell me, who were -- who was present at those meetings when you attended?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, I attended collegium meetings, that is to say, of the collegium of the corps commander, up until the 30th of March. After that, from time to time, I went to the commander for briefings. At those meetings where I was present, at the collegium of the corps commander, all members of the collegium attended, all members of the collegium of the corps commander. Now, who were these members? That is established in a document, very specifically. I can mention their names, but during -- over time, the names changed, depending on who had what duty. But I know the organisational entities, who the members of the collegium were, and I can tell you that, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Who were the members of the collegium? Yes. Please -- please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, in addition to the commander, the members of the collegium were the other -- the following persons ex officio: The Chief of Staff of the corps, the assistant commander of the corps for information and morale, the assistant commander of the corps for logistics, the assistant commander of the corps for security matters, the assistant commander of the corps for personnel and housing affairs, and I don't know. I may have omitted someone or maybe I've mentioned them all. Those were the persons involved -- or rather, the persons who headed these functions were members of the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from the 24th of March throughout the conflict, how often did these meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 24th of March, 1999 and onwards, I don't know how the collegium meetings of the commander went, but I know that I had meetings that I attended in order to present a briefing. Sometimes it was every seven days, sometimes every ten days or so, and sometimes perhaps even more often, depending on the needs involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also talked about other meetings; in other words, not collegium meetings, where you would brief the corps commander. Were these meetings just between yourself and the corps commander, or were there other members of the corps command present as well?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, most often the commander would call me to the command post to issue me an assignment or for me to brief him about the state of affairs in the garrison command and in my group. Most often I was the only person in attendance. Perhaps it may have been somebody else too, but I didn't notice. For the most part, it was only me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you spoke about the people that would be attending the collegium meetings. For example, the Chief of Staff and the assistant commander for information and morale. What was the name of the assistant commander for information and morale?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander for information and morale was Colonel Mirko Starcevic, and then Colonel Dragisa Marinkovic took over from him. Colonel Starcevic went to a new duty; he became assistant commander for morale in the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How about the assistant commander for security affairs? What would his -- what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security was Momir Stojanovic, father's name Bogoljub.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, at these meetings where you attended, I take it that each person responsible for their department would brief General Lazarevic on the situation within their department. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that General Lazarevic would in turn brief the corps command about the state of the -- state of the war and the -- the efficiency or the effectiveness of the Pristina Corps Command operations. Is that also right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, things developed along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also said in evidence that at these meetings there would be discussions or there would be reminders that international humanitarian law should be adhered to. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that these reminders would come -- would be made every day.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, very often. Very often. From this time distance, I cannot say whether it was actually every day, but it was that often that it seemed like every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was it at every occasion when the corps command met?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell you exactly whether it was absolutely every occasion, but it was very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you also said that there was foreign media and you were able to through the foreign media establish what was happening within Pristina and also within Kosovo. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not right. It is not right. We had our own system of information in the corps command, and foreign media for the most part we did not follow. We did not listen to that. Only sometimes if someone would get some information from that. However, our system of information was based on the system of information of the army and our state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness already answered, and in my modest view, there was no foundation or basis for that kind of a question to be put by the Prosecutor. Having listened to this witness's testimony yesterday very carefully, I did not ever hear him say that his information was based on the foreign media. But he has already responded, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just for the record would note that yesterday the witness did talk about foreign correspondence criss-crossing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, during these meetings, I take it that there were discussions about allegations of crimes that may have been committed by members of the VJ. Did those discussions ever take place?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I was a member of the collegium until the 30th of March. It is possible that that was discussed too. From this time distance, I cannot remember that. But for the most part, in view of my functional duty, I focused on personnel matters. And that is what I was most interested in and that is what I paid attention to; namely, what my own tasks were from that point of view and what I was supposed to do about that. The rest was very important, but it did not preoccupy my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't actually ask what was your focus, but you agree that at the meetings, at some of the meetings that you attended, allegations of crimes committed by the VJ were discussed within that group. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. From this time distance, I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what kind of allegations were discussed? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
