utterances.text: Well, for the most part, organisational problems were discussed. Our tasks related to defence, related to the combat training of units, for taking measures in relation to morale, discipline, and order, then various personnel matters, and many other topical tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I appreciate what you're saying; however, I want to concentrate on the discussion regarding allegations of crimes committed by the VJ. And what I want to know is what kind of information, what kind of allegations were discussed at the meetings or at a meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we have already got a clear answer to this question. This is the second or third time that the question is being repeated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I respectfully disagree. My -- I submit that I have a basis to ask a further question about the subject matter of the allegations, considering the witness did say that -- that these allegations were discussed or there was a possibility that these allegations were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's as high as it goes, possibly. However, questions of this nature often elicit further information, so please proceed with this question. If it's unproductive, then move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm guided, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, leaving aside what was usually discussed at these meetings, with respect, as you said, to -- to other measures related to morale and discipline, I want you to cast your mind back to the information that may have been discussed about allegations of crimes committed by the VJ. Can you tell the Court what kind of information was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember anything like -- anything like that. I know that many terrorist acts were discussed in which our units and members of the corps sustained losses. But as for these allegations that you are asking me about, I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you remember that there were reminders of -- reminders to adhere to international humanitarian law. Why were these reminders made at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those meetings -- now, this is my assumption, my conclusion -- the people were reminded so that it be always at the forefront of their mind, so that the officers could inform their subordinates about that. And the logic behind it was probably that if you keep drumming something in, repeating something, then it tends to stick in people's minds more than if you never discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you, Colonel, that these reminders were made because in fact the VJ were indeed committing crimes throughout Pristina and Kosovo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is absolutely not true --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the foundation is for this claim that is now put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The foundation is the inference that could be drawn from the regular reference to the obligation to comply with international humanitarian law. There is a basis for the question. So please continue, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't think you answered my question, or at least it's not recorded in the transcript. What is your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it. I would kindly ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that the reminders to adhere to international humanitarian law were made because the VJ were indeed committing crimes throughout Pristina and Kosovo and Metohija. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say not only that I don't agree with that. I can say that this is not so. Particularly when it comes to the town of Pristina. And it is not correct if you look at the whole of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your evidence is that there were no crimes, no violations of international humanitarian law in Pristina during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. I am saying that if crimes were committed - and I don't know that they were, because I didn't hear about that - they were not committed by the army. And in particular, not in the town of Pristina. I mentioned Pristina because I am really familiar with the situation there; I know it best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So your evidence is that no member of the Pristina Corps within Pristina committed crimes.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am claiming here that such crimes were not committed by the army in Pristina and that I don't know of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What crimes are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not talking about crimes. You are talking about crimes. Yesterday and today I spoke about the crimes committed by the terrorists. And as to what crimes you're talking about, I don't know. Please do ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know of crimes that were committed in Pristina by either members of the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned yesterday that General Lazarevic -- you met with General Lazarevic on the 27th of April, 1999. And you -- you said that you had asked him to come and visit the garrison. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you said that he was not able to come that evening because he was busy. Do you know why he was busy?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't tell you that, because I didn't know that at the time and I don't know it now. And the commander is not duty-bound to tell his subordinates why he was busy, but of course if he wants to do so, he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at some point you went with General Lazarevic to the Grand Hotel. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you went there, who else was present in the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember all the persons who were there in the Grand Hotel. I know that there was the chairwoman of the Kolo Srpskih Sestara, Mrs. Pavlovic. I think -- I'm not sure, that there were some people from the media. I think that Colonel Starcevic was also there. Perhaps some other people too. But I didn't really try and remember that. These are the people that I remember, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How often would you go to the Grand Hotel during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the conflict, apart from that one occasion, as far as I can recall, never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But parts of the Pristina Corps were located in the Grand Hotel, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only those elements that I told you about were actually stationed in the Grand Hotel, and that would be the information centre and that was the place where mail was exchanged. And the other floors were used by the Sloga hotel company from Pristina. It is possible that those premises were used by some other companies that actually rented it from Sloga, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could go back to Exhibit 5D00348, please. And, Colonel, this is the document with respect to your garrison, which we discussed earlier. And at the bottom of the page, in the penultimate paragraph, it says, and I'll read it: "As necessitated and in keeping with the situation, accommodate the group in the general area of -- of the Pristina municipality, the municipal court, and the premises of the PrK command, including the Grand Hotel." And my question is: What part of the group that is listed here was accommodated in the Grand Hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me explain this to you. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you explain it, would you read that paragraph, please. Could you read it aloud to us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. "The group is to be deployed according to the need and in accordance with the situation in the broader sector of the Pristina Municipal Assembly, the municipal court, and the building of the PrK Command with the Grand Hotel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were going to explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an area that forms a triangle. The corners are the municipal assembly, the municipal court, and the Grand Hotel, the PrK Command. This is the way in which an area for the deployment both of units and of commands is defined in the military. So the command -- the commander gave me the task to, in this area that is bordered by those -- those points, deploy my command; and that's what I did. I did it in such a way that I really deployed them in this triangle, but no elements were deployed in any of the buildings that are used to define this triangular area; in other words, they were not deployed in the Grand Hotel, in the municipal assembly, because they were housed in a building adjacent to the municipal assembly and some were also housed in a hut. So it was -- they were deployed in this area as it was defined, not in the buildings themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So from these three subgroups, including the command group, the military court, and the group of the operations centre with the department for air space situation reporting, none of those groups were deployed in the Grand Hotel. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that none of these groups, none of these elements were in the Grand Hotel. Moreover, in accordance with this phrase "in accordance with the need," that -- in accordance with the basic concept of the commander, I deployed some elements to an -- to an area 50 metres away from this area, in the basement of the sports centre Boro i Ramiz, close to the corps command building but not in the buildings themselves. This is close to the Pristina stadium, the football club Pristina. That was the air surveillance element.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in addition to the Pristina Corps Command, there was also a military battalion --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not next to but ... No. No, no battalion. There was no battalion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But there was a Military Police Battalion in Pristina, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military Police Battalion existed as a unit of the Pristina Corps, and after the aggression started, in accordance with its own plan, it was deployed in an area defined by those plans. And for the most part, I was not aware of the location, but I do know that its task was inter alia to secure the corps command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did the Military Battalion -- Military Police Battalion also provide security to the garrison?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the garrison -- or as far as the garrison facilities are concerned, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was the strength of this Military Police Battalion, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I sit here, I can say it was somewhere between 350 and 400 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that all of these people were armed as well.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you remember yesterday we discussed -- or it was discussed about the artillery from Vranjevac being fired at the village of Koljevac [phoen]. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Kojlovica. That's what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in relation to the town of Pristina, it's correct, isn't it, that the -- these two villages, Vranjevac and Kojlovica are situated on an elevated position.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vranjevac itself is partly in the low grounds and some are in -- on the high ground. But Vranjevac as a whole is a residential area and -- between one and another house it is not more than 5 metres. The streets are narrow, maybe 2 to 3 metres wide. The village of Kojlovica is not on the high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But compared to the centre of town, it would be elevated, both those places. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- not Kojlovica, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And from the centre of town or from the area of -- of Pristina town, it would be possible to -- to see the village of Vranjevac, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the centre of Pristina -- well, depending on where you are in the centre, because there are quite a few tall buildings in the centre. It -- you have a line of sight to just parts of Vranjevac, not the whole of Vranjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually would like to show the witness a map that was marked by one of the witnesses in the Prosecution case, and I ask leave to do that because it was not on my initial list. And the reason why I had not put it on my list was that I did not anticipate the detail that my learned friend would go into with respect to the markings of where her house was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection as a matter of principle, because my humble opinion now is that an exception is becoming a rule now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't assist the Chamber. If you would address the issue that's advanced that because you went into some detail in this, it's only right that the evidence that we've heard about the matter should be put to the witness. And as a general principle of fairness, it's even a question of being fair to the -- the witness, as well as to the interests of justice and to the witness who previously gave evidence here. Now, what do you have to say to that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not opposed to the map being shown. My colleague gave me a map that was not announced earlier as an exhibit, and I agree with him that it might be exhibited during the testimony of witness Filipovic. I agreed to that. But this objection of mine was submitted as a matter of principle, as I have already said. As for this map, the map that I was given a hard copy of, I do not oppose that because -- although it does not have an IC number at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're -- well, does it have a number and is it already part of the process?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The ICU map that I want to show is -- is indeed -- does have a number. It's IC 15. But my learned friend is right that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Just -- just a second. Now, the principle on which you're standing is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're talking about two maps, and I agreed that my colleague show a map that is unmarked and does not have an IC number. That is what we agreed upon before he started and I'm not opposed to that. I fully agree to any other proposals related to Pristina maps, irrespective of when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is the objection in principle that you take?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw any -- my objection, if any. Maybe I misunderstood what was going on. Maybe Mr. Fila wishes to answer something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will add only in one sentence what the concern of the Defence is. As you know, I never objected to any documents submitted by the Prosecution. What concerns me and us is that your rule that when the oath is taken, the documents have to be stated, the ones that are going to be used in cross-examination have been -- has been subjected to many exceptions. It's not the exceptions that I'm worried about, but by the waste of time. If anybody's interested in time here - in addition to yourself, Your Honour, of course - it is me; I hate wasting time. There is this unnecessary discussion about every such document, translated, not translated, is needed, is not needed, surprised, not surprised. Why are we surprised by anything at this stage? I would only be surprised if they were to give up on Sainovic altogether. I cannot be surprised by anything else. We've been through everything so far. That is what I wanted to say by way of a caution. That is what we discussed amongst ourselves. That is what we talked to the colleagues. I don't really want to waste time. And now you've wasted time on account of me, too. We've lost time on account of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that sounds to me more like a expression of frustration rather than a carefully formulated legal objection. Mr. Cepic would have a foundation for an objection in principle if he could demonstrate to us that the Prosecution ought to have foreseen the detailed exploration of the relative locations of Kojlovica and Vranjevac. The Prosecution tell us that they could not foresee that from the notice given and sought therefore, in fairness to all involved, to present the map which was marked by an earlier witness on precisely this point. Now, if there is no reason to object on that basis, then all our time has been wasted by a frivolous objection based on a principle that I am yet unable to -- to divine. So we shall further avoid the waste of any further time and proceed with the Prosecution putting this document to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If I could first ask for the ICU -- the -- the map that was marked by the witness, which I recall was IC 148. If that could be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday you marked this map and -- and figure number 2 was -- was what you said was the location of Mrs. Bala's house. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It's the house in Lapski Street, number 30 Lapski Street.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked Lapska Street; although, I -- I underline that once again. I said yesterday that this is a very poor map for orientation. For such a serious occasion -- I do apologise to the Trial Chamber, but this is really a caricature of a map. I have some maps with me, I have some topographic maps, too, and the rest. We'll try with this one. There's no problem with that. I put all the circles there. That's true. But it is a very poor map for this kind of orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the evidence that the witness gave herself in court -- I'm going to show you where she marked her house. If I could have IC 15, please. Is it possible to have them side-by-side? Now, you would agree, Witness, that the circle that Mrs. Bala had marked as her residence is just above the -- the bazaar, the market? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This circle that was drawn here was drawn here but not by the old market. What is very important here is the old market. This is no old market. This is the current market, before the aggression and during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a completely different market. The old market is a completely different market. But never mind. Even if she lived there, even from that place, she can see Vranjevac even less -- or rather, I beg your pardon, Kojlovica. Even less. She can see Kojlovica even less from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you agree with the possibility that if she was on the top of her building, that being a five-storey building, that her view would be enhanced with respect to Vranjevac?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the top of the building, it is only logical that there is a better view than from the ground level. However, irrespective of that, one cannot see Kojlovica. The village of Kojlovica cannot be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: My question was referring to Vranjevac. And would you agree with me also, Colonel -- would you agree with me also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if your -- if your question does relate to Vranjevac -- Vranjevac, we must have an answer to it. So can you answer that, please, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vranjevac can be seen. Not all of it, though. Most parts of Vranjevac can be seen, because Vranjevac is on some slopes. And on this elevation, to the north of the railroad between Pristina and Podujevo. However, Lapska Street was Lapska during the time of the aggression, where it was. It cannot be moved anywhere else. Where the circle is, that is where Lapska Street never was. I have a map here of the hotel as well, a map of Pristina from that period of time. That is not where Lapska Street is. Lapska Street goes from the area of the railroad towards the interior of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I -- I didn't ask you about Lapska Street. I'm simply asking from that location that is marked on this map, marked by the witness herself, there is a view --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that location, one can see Vranjevac; or rather, most parts of Vranjevac, but not Kojlovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it you also agree that with binoculars the view would be even further enhanced from the top of that building.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With binoculars, the view can be much better, but not Kojlovica. Kojlovica cannot be seen even with astronomical binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you agree with me that from that location, from the top of her building at that location, she would have been able to see into the centre of town. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of the centre of town, yes; those that are not overshadowed by taller buildings. Because in Pristina there are even 15-storey buildings and her building has only 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you know of the -- the Jugopetrol warehouse in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand. Could you please repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Wasn't there a Jugopetrol warehouse, a fuel depot in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And was it not located near the Pristina Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "nearby" is a relative thing. This is where it was: It was near the Orthodox cemetery of Pristina. Well, it was about 150 to 200 metres away from that cemetery. It was about 100 metres away from the main road going from Urosevac via Pristina to Kosovska Mitrovica. I think that that's the depot that you're asking me about. If it is that depot, then it is where I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this Jugopetrol warehouse, this fuel depot, are you able to say how many fuel tankers it -- it consisted of or -- or how large the complex was?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, because I really don't know that or was that within the scope of my work. I used to know a person called Lalic who was the director. That is what I can tell you about that depot. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that the military would -- would obtain its fuel from that depot. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, because that was not within the scope of my work, but I do know that the army on the basis of contracts and plans of the ministry got supplies according to a certain scheme from the territory of the entire state. As for this warehouse, this depot, whether fuel was obtained for the army from there, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But I take it -- I take it you agree that fuel was obviously important for the running of the army, especially during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuel was very important. And we did get fuel supplies from the territory of our country. What else could we do but get supplies of fuel in order to defend our country?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so it's likely that if there was a fuel depot such as what we've been discussing, it's likely that the military would -- would be taking fuel from that depot. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, but it had the legitimate right to get these supplies. But whether it was precisely from there and whether that is what the plans said, well, that is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If we could go back to Exhibit P2004, please. Witness, this is a document that we're familiar with. If you look down the bottom, it says that "On the night of the 12th and 13th of April, the following installations in Pristina -- in the Pristina sector were hit." And then there's a sentence that says: "The following civilian targets were attacked in Pristina," and one of them is the Jugopetrol warehouse. I suggest to you that the Jugopetrol warehouse was not a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that the Jugopetrol depot or warehouse was a civilian target. Well, the army drinks water too, so probably the waterworks therefore become a military objective. Nearby Badovac, near Pristina, that is where the waterworks were bombed. Probably these people were guided by the fact that the military drink water too. If that logic were to be applied, then there cannot be a single target that would not be hit. Water was drunk by the military and by the population, Serbs, Siptars, Turks, Roma, we all drank water. And then we're wondering why the population was moving out, the Serb and the Siptar population. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you must -- you must agree with me that a facility such as this one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got his answer. I mean, we'll assess the answer in the light of all the evidence. We need to move on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for Prosecution Exhibit 1996 to be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the -- this is the record of minutes at a meeting held by the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija in Pristina on the 7th of May, 1999. And as you will see from the front page, the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Sainovic, attended the meeting, in addition -- in addition to various officials from the MUP. And I'd like you -- I'd like to go to page 5 of the English, please, and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can see that he read "Sainovic" for some reason. I mean, the Prosecutor. But I see no reason why this document should be shown to the Pristina Corps commander, who is an officer of the Yugoslav Army, except if you need confirmation for the umpteenth time that Mr. Sainovic attended this meeting. I don't know why we are honoured in this way. The witness is an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia and he should be asked whether this meeting took place and how and why, but what is the foundation for that? So I object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're being unduly sensitive, Mr. Fila, because no question has yet been asked, and I don't at the moment know what the purpose of this is, and there's certainly no evidence against Mr. Fila [sic] contained in what's been said so far. Mr. Cepic, you also wish to object?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only if you allow me, Your Honours. As far as I can remember, my client, General Lazarevic, was not allowed to explain this document in the course of his examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me a --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The explanation was that he did not attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- well, please be quiet for the moment, would you, until we deal with the situation. There's been an objection taken. They wish to prevent you answering, because they think it's unfair to their client, so you mustn't intervene in that -- in that situation. Can you give me a transcript reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I will try to do my best. In next three minutes we will have that reference, please, or earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it needs to be now, because -- or as quickly as you can, because you wish to oppose the question even being addressed, which is ... Well, perhaps we should hear what the question is, first of all, and then you can let me know whether you insist on the objection. Mr. Sachdeva, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You will see, Colonel, on this page that the -- the chief -- the chief of the SUP in Pristina, Mr. Janicevic, is giving a report. And I want you to look down at the middle of the page, or towards the latter part of the page. Do you see where it says: "The military is not taking sufficient measures and most crimes are being perpetrated by VJ members"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is your purpose in relying on this document to put your question? When you've had answers to this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's an issue of credibility. The witness who was -- who was in Pristina throughout the whole war period has given evidence to the Court that he does not know of any crimes that were committed in Pristina by VJ members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. So his evidence is clear. So what are you now trying to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm trying to show the witness that there is a report that -- by the -- by the Ministry of the Interior that the VJ members were committing crimes. I'm simply going to ask him whether that causes him to reflect on his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. He's already answered the matter clearly. You're putting, yet again, a matter that's already been put. This system does not allow for the putting to every witness of every document of any nature in the case that might -- that might contradict his answer. You will have an opportunity to make submissions about the value to be placed on this in relation to his evidence and his evidence in relation to this in due course. So please go to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm guided, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday we -- we discussed this leaflet by the KLA. You remember that? Allegedly by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you remember that it appeared to emanate from the president of the Republic of Kosovo, Mr. Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who that originated from. I don't know that. But the flyer was found there. And that was not the only one; there were several. And secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just -- just one moment. Please ask a question, because I think I've already explained to you that this method, which we're all familiar with in -- in common-law jurisdictions of establishing a basis for a question by asking witnesses to confirm things, where the witness that we have -- the witnesses we've experienced here want to answer and deal with all the nuances that might -- might be behind the question, does not help us to make progress. It helps in this system to get to the nub of the matter quickly. So please ask the question. We -- we took the same line with -- with a number of Defence counsel questions in cross-examination of Prosecution witnesses earlier, particularly in Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination. Again, you are coming from a fairly similar jurisdictions and are familiar with an approach which does not suit the type of evidence or the experience of -- of the witnesses that we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, you don't know who produced this document, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can only assume or speculate that it came from the terrorist centres; but I don't know. I don't know who wrote those leaflets that were thrown out of the plane. I really don't know that. But they were not thrown from our planes. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you -- are you saying this document was thrown from a plane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was just one in the context of the leaflets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see how -- you see how easy it is to cause confusion by not just concentrating on the question and answering the question you're being asked. Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You don't know, Witness, do you, whether it was produced by the VJ or from Belgrade? You don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My army would never have done that. It never did that, and this I rule out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have a reference for this interesting claim in order to make it easier for us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the -- your objection is -- is far too late. The witness had answered the question before you were getting to your feet. And had you done so, the answer might have been different, but the question has been answered. And I'm sure you're not unhappy with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not because of the answer, but just so that I know for future reference. Maybe I have simply missed something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't based on -- on evidence. It's a -- it's a question which simply asked the witness to confirm that he doesn't know a particular source. But I -- it certainly didn't strike me as a suggestion that there was evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I am -- yes. Mr. Sachdeva, I -- if there had been objection taken to that question, it would have been sustained. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Colonel, you told the Court that you were in Pristina, apart from that one day, from the onset of the conflict until the end of the conflict. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you've given evidence about KLA activities in Pristina and also in the general area of Pristina, and you've given the Court a lot of information about which positions in Pristina were hit by NATO. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you are in a position to have known what was taking place in Pristina during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in a position to know everything that happened in Pristina, things that I saw, things that I myself experienced, and things that were within the purview of my job. Many things that were outside of my purview were not something that I had to know and were not something that I could know, but most of the things that were within my purview, well, I was informed about them. I knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it the -- the bakery shops were not within your purview. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, bakery shops were not within my purview, but that doesn't mean that our families -- my family, for one, bought bread there to eat. And during the war I was in contact with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I take it that also the -- the functioning of the -- the pension office was not within your purview, as it related to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that relates to civilians, but many family members of mine were pensioners, many of my friends, and I had many Siptar friends. They received their pensions. There were retired officers, Siptars, my very good friends, who received their pensions. There were those who became renegades, who became terrorists. And I had some very good friends and they told me about that and I saw them when they received their pensions, because the cashiers' desks where they received the pensions were very close to where I was at the Union Theatre, 100 metres away from there, this is where makeshift offices were put up after NATO air-strikes. And that's all I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that there were, if I'm right, two train stations within the general area of Pristina. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the territory of the municipality of Pristina, there was only one train station, not two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And given that you have a -- a fair amount of knowledge as to what was going on in Pristina, you must have seen the hundreds of civilians taking those trains away from Pristina. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You must have known about it through other means. You must have heard about the civilians that were leaving Pristina on the trains on a regular basis during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about people leaving Pristina on a regular basis. I did hear about people leaving it by train, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that's what my question was. So you heard that there were hundreds of people -- I put it to you that you must have heard that there were hundreds of people leaving by the train, leaving Pristina, on a regular basis throughout the war. You agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with the claim that they were leaving on a regular basis, and I don't agree that I heard a figure, but I did hear that people were moving out of Pristina by train, and I also know that they -- that the inhabitants of Pristina left it by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And those inhabitants who were leaving by bus and by train, they were Albanian civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Both Siptars and Serbs, and in fact Turks and Roma left it too. I know that trains were used by Siptars more often than by Serbs in order to flee NATO air-strikes, and buses were used more often by Serbs. But one can conclude that all modes of traffic were used by the population as it moved out of Pristina, and members of all ethnic groups did so. That would be my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, it's just an assumption on your part that they were leaving because of NATO strikes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not an assumption on my part. I personally know some of these, and I participated in some elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Do you really want to ask that question at this stage in this examination when you've heard already the witness's position on it? We know it's a controversial issue. All the evidence will have to be assessed. Have you got much more cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Not much more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- Mr. President, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already dealt with fleeing to some extent, but -- well, I suppose if you're not allowed to continue, then no doubt there'll be re-examination. So perhaps you better continue with this and clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you did not speak to every single Albanian civilian that was leaving by train or buses, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, there's a limit to how many -- I mean, some questions are just silly. There comes a point really when we have the law of diminishing returns in cross-examination. Do you really seriously think that that's a reasonable question to ask in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm just trying to establish the basis for his knowledge, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you ask that question. Let's hear what the answer is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What's the basis for your knowledge as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. The question was: Did you speak to every single Albanian civilian that was leaving by train or bus? What's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is elicirate [as interpreted] to expect me to do so, even if I wanted to. Sometimes as I passed by I would speak to some of them on this topic, asking them why they were leaving, why they were leaving on -- in those columns, not moving out. And I told you what the answer was I got from them. They said, "I -- we don't know when -- where we're going." This is -- this pertains to the columns that passed by my headquarters of my command. Some other columns, some other people who were moving out were motivated by other reasons. They would have given other explanations. I don't know what these explanations were. I don't know nothing about that. So I was only talking about those things that I know of. As regards people moving out, I can tell you that I participated and I assisted in the -- I assisted those people to move out. I am sorry that I did so. I may have overstepped the boundaries of my powers, but in accordance with the basic concept of the corps commander, indicating that civilians should be assisted, when the manager of the public bus company, Mrs. Murganic, I gave a certain amount of fuel when she said that citizens want to move their women, their children, and their elderly urgently. And I approved that some fuel could be dispensed in this way so that people could move out to Nis and to other parts of Serbia in -- because people wanted to protect their children, their women, and the elderly. And that's what I did, and that's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And those Albanian citizens that were leaving Pristina, they were being escorted by members of the VJ, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Or actually, I never saw that, and I was never informed of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would this be a convenient time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Then just before we rise, there's been some indication, Mr. Ivetic, that you have a problem with tomorrow's proposed schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With the extent -- with the extent it's sitting, although I don't know to what extent Mr. Delic will start today, we have the possibility that we might be coming up for an hour or so of cross-examination of Mr. Delic, who is another one of the witnesses that I had to pick up for Mr. Lukic, and I don't know the status of Mr. Lukic at present, but I suspect that will -- I've been preparing as if I will have to handle this witness. It's the witness for which we have 14 days' worth of transcripts for Milosevic and a number of exhibits just for purposes of the direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's your -- if that's your concern, he is scheduled for six hours, so there's little or no prospect that you would have to cross-examine him tomorrow. Unless that were to change significantly. And at that stage, if -- if we came to the end of his evidence in chief, then would be the time to raise the concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To raise it. I can -- I guess I can agree with that, for the purposes of that aspect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. -- yes, Mr. Ivetic -- sorry, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, perhaps the reason I'm going to mention is a far more banal one, but some of our colleagues have already booked flights, and I think that Mr. Fila already bought a ticket to fly to Belgrade tomorrow at 6.00, in order to use this weekend to spend it at home with their families. Perhaps it's a much simpler reason, but that would be the motive. Could our sitting hours be at least half an hour shorter so that they could make it on time and catch that flight? Even at the expense of the break, if necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble is that we don't have that flexibility. We can't not have these breaks, for reasons of interpretation, and we can't get into the courtroom earlier than 2.15, unless something happens. So -- now, if -- the reason we thought it would be possible to do this is until yesterday, late yesterday -- and you must have thought we were sitting tomorrow afternoon anyway. So I'm surprised that travel arrangements have been made so quickly. But our court schedule was for tomorrow afternoon. We were forced out of the morning to accommodate the Prlic trial, which is dealing with a videolink. I know that earlier it was in the morning, but it was changed to the afternoon last week. So if -- if -- I mean, Mr. Fila, is this something you've done since yesterday evening, made an arrangement since yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you can see, there's two of us. So I'm going to leave at any rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I -- so I think we will sit that day as scheduled. I mean, I have a travel arrangement myself, which isn't far away from that, and I anticipate making it. So we will sit according to the schedule that was intimated tomorrow. We'll rise now. Mr. Filipovic, we need to break again, and we will resume at ten past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that -- that's the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic, you gave evidence about a -- the lack of damage to religious buildings in Pristina. Are you familiar with a mosque known as the Emperor's Mosque?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am very familiar with that mosque. I finished high school 10 metres away from that mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it burned on the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of June? What year?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that; although, I was in Pristina then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've seen a photograph showing it burning and been told that that was on the 15th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was even close to my command post. I would have had to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's look then at P1789 and at page 9. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I see that it's the mosque. It's probably that one. Otherwise, I cannot tell by anything whether that's the mosque or whether it's another mosque, but I see the minaret and the mosque. You can see the mosque in the background, but I'm not sure that the part you can see in front is the mosque. The mosque is the minaret and what is right next to the minaret. As for the right-hand part of the picture where the flames are, that's not the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is it the historical archive of the Islamic community?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. That's where a similar building was, and close to it is Sahat Kula, the watch-tower. But it is not the mosque. It is a building, but it is not the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say, though, that you -- were you were based near there. You cannot tell me if this is the Islamic community's historical archive?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. It may be that. I know some facilities individually, but I don't know whether that was precisely the archive of the Islamic community. I know that building very well. I remember it very well. 10 or 15 metres away from it is the Orthodox clock tower, Sahat Kula.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it possible you knew this building as the Islamic library?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know that, but I know the building. I know that it was there, and I know that it was not used for residential purposes. There was an institution there, but I really did not know at the time what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a brief question, with your leave, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, it's me again. You mentioned that the military territorial detachments were re-subordinated to the Pristina Corps. Do you know whether some brigades were also re-subordinated to the Pristina Corps? Apart from the basic units.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the military district, the 202nd base, there were brigades too. The 252nd Armoured Brigade from the 1st Army, the 211th Armoured Brigade from the Nis Army, and some other brigades too, the 175th, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Colonel. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these buildings, they were guarded by English soldiers after KFOR got in. I'm sorry, I have to say that. The mosque near my command post was secured by English soldiers. They even had sandbags there. And there was this place behind the sandbags, and that is where English soldiers from KFOR were on guard duty. I personally saw that. They were about 50 metres away from this building. As a matter of fact, close to that location, counting on the reliability of the English soldiers from KFOR, one citizen near the mosque, Dragan Lazic, left his car for them to take care of and his car disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be of some significance for you to know that the evidence we have is that this happened that day shortly before the arrival of KFOR. Thank you. That completes your evidence, Mr. Filipovic. I thank you for coming to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, and good evening to all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is General Bozidar Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak to truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good evening.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, you -- it was a long wait, but we begin finally. Could you please tell me for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: I am retired General Bozidar Delic, father's name Nikola.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please give me only the major posts that you held during your military career.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: During my military career, I performed all the command functions from the platoon commander level to the corps commander level. At the end of my military career, I was in the General Staff of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. I was the deputy chief of the operations administration, and I was the chief of the operations administration at one point and I retired from that post, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What military schools did you graduate from?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: I have all the military schools in the JNA: The military academy of the ground forces in Belgrade and Sarajevo; the command and staff school in Belgrade; and the National Defence School, the war college, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, what is your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: I am a deputy, a member of parliament in the Serbian parliament or assembly, and I am the deputy speaker of that assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please tell us, what duties did you have in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, I was the commander of the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us, what were the chief activities of your brigade in 1998 and 1999, up until the beginning of the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: The chief tasks of my brigade were as follows: First of all, to train and educate soldiers. That was up until a time in 1998. Securing military facilities and installations, securing the state border, primarily the in-depth security of the state border, and ensuring that all the roads in my area are passable. What I said about the training of the soldiers, up until March of 1998 the basic training of the soldiers was done in my brigade, but as of March 1998, up until the end of the aggression, we only carried out the second stage of the training; the basic training was carried out in other units outside of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You mentioned the securing of the state border. I would like to know, what was the length of the border belt at the state border that was secured by the units of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: The units of my brigade secured the larger or the largest part of the border with the Republic of Albania and a part of the border with the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, as it is called. All in all, it would be about 150 kilometres of state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit number 5D877.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this document that you see in front of you, is this a document that originated from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document dated February. It was drafted in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What are these dates here? So we start with the second passage. Could you just please tell us very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Here where we have the dates, all the dates are in January. These are the border incidents on the state border in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We see that there is a substantial number of those in January. Could you please tell us: As the aggression loomed near, did the number of border incidents increase?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1999, despite the OSCE presence, virtually every day there would be those border incidents. I can see that we have 13 of those listed here. And they continued on in January and February, March, all the way up to the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could you please explain to me very briefly what was the procedure when a border incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: The border was secured by small units, seven to eight people strong. There would be six to seven soldiers and one officer, commanding officer. The procedure was as follows: If it was apparent that these people carried weapons, they would be stopped. If -- in fact, they would be stopped if they carried weapons, they would be asked to drop [Realtime transcript read in error "draw"] the weapons, to put their hands up, and to surrender. What I say here about them carrying weapons, I say that because if they did not carry weapons, they would be violating the state border regime and they would be treated in a different manner. If they fired on the people securing the border, which would be most often the case, fire would be returned in order to neutralise them, capture them. In some situations the purpose would be to prevent them from getting into our territory or, in the final analysis, to destroy such a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Cepic. I assume that line 20 the word should be "asked to drop the weapons." Should it? If you intercepted someone carrying a weapon, you would ask them to do what with the weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To drop their weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The order was to drop the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, if there was an incident, did the investigative organs of the OSCE mission go to the site or anyone else, in fact?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: If you're talking -- if you're asking me about 1998, there is a difference between 1998 and 1999 -- or rather, there is a difference between what happened in 1998 until May and afterwards, for the rest of 1998. When there was an incident, especially if there were any casualties among the army troops or among the terrorists or those who violated the state border regime, an investigative judge would visit the scene. He was supposed to come from the Nis military garrison. Crime scene technicians from my brigade would also go to the scene, and a local mixed commission would also be summoned from our organs and also from Albania. That was how it was until sometime in May. After that, the contacts ceased and the local mixed commissions from Albania refused to come to the scene of those incidents. And once the OSCE mission was in place, it was notified of any -- of all such incidents and they tried to visit all the scenes of such border incidents. There were some problems, because there was a large number of such border incidents, and it was a mountainous area in wintertime. So the teams which were supposed to come from Prizren were sometimes unable to arrive at the scene in the same day, because they had gone somewhere else to verify some other incidents. So they would then come the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We have seen some footage of a border incident at Liken Mountain. We heard General Maisonneuve, who testified about that. Now I would like to move on to something else related to 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system 5D683, please. Actually, 863.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you see this document that's in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document from 1998 originating from my brigade, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see here in item 1 that prior to opening fire, an assessment should be made whether there are any monitors from the international community present there. Now, my question to you is: What was your relationship with the foreign monitors and observers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: It was a correct relationship on both sides, from our side, and in most cases, from their side too. We were responsible for their security and safety. In fact, our state was. And we, as the representatives of the army, and also the representatives of the police, we were duty-bound to ensure that within our areas they can move about and that they are safe, lest there should be any unpleasant situations or lest the worst-case scenario should come true, lest there should be any casualties. And as far as I know, only two of the mission members were wounded, because they activated a mine that had been laid by the terrorists and they were wounded. As far as I know, throughout their presence in Kosovo and Metohija, none of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, what was the basis for this order that you issued?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This order was issued pursuant to an order from the Pristina Corps, and this order is actually referenced here. The number is listed here, and the date is the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, we heard that you said that there was an increase in border incidents. Were there any incidents in the hinterland up until the beginning of the aggression?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Well, I and my brigade were in charge of the border most of all. I referred to the situation at the border in that order. But throughout Kosovo and Metohija, there was an increase of incidents in 1999. Most of these incidents took place on the roads. Both civilian vehicles and police vehicles, the latter in particular, and the army vehicles, came under attack, came across mines, or were targeted by hand-held rocket launchers, and so on. And something that is peculiar for this period: A large number of Albanians, loyal citizens of the Republic of Serbia, were killed in that period, as were Albanians who in late 1998, sometime in September or October, surrendered their weapons to the army or the police. The OSCE received daily reports and so did we, and bodies of those Albanians were found in many locations throughout Kosovo and Metohija, including my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, could you please clarify, where were you born and where did you spend a substantial part of your life?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: I was born in the vicinity of Djakovica, and that's where I lived until I completed my secondary school. When I left to study at the military academy, and up until 1995, I only went there to visit my parents on my annual leave. And from 1995 onwards, from the 6th of February, 1995, I came to the Prizren garrison, to the 549th Brigade, where I was first the Chief of Staff, and then from August of 1997, I was the commander of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit number 5D878, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the document to appear on our screens, before the war, was -- were there zones that were under the control of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. In some territories, from the beginning of 1998, but especially in February and March, there were a few territories that were under the control of the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us briefly, in your own area of responsibility, very briefly, which territories were under the control of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility, especially the territory that is near Djakovica, that is the territory that includes the villages of Glodjane, Jablanica, Kraljane, Crmljane, Bec. Then another territory near Orahovac, that is the territory that included the villages from Gornji and Donji Potocani via Drenovac to the village of Zatrice and the village of Petkovic. Then the entire territory around Malisevo. Then the territory, sometime from June 1998, the territory of the villages of -- well, the villages that are in the triangle of roads, so to speak: Zerze-Prizren, Prizren-Suva Reka, Suva Reka-Orahovac, not to mention all of them specifically. Gornje and Donje Ratimlje, Studencane, Samodreza, not to mention all of them. Then Veljka Hoca, Mala Hoca, Celine, Brestovac, Ratimlje, Nogovac. And a territory around Suva Reka, which is a territory that had Budakovo in its central part, but it's Budakovo, Macitevo, it's that mountainous area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. What was the situation in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In 1999, as I've already said, from the beginning of 1999 the terrorists, despite the presence of the OSCE mission, staged incidents every day and they extended the territory that they kept under their control in relation to the territory that they held sometime in July 1998. So in my assessment, already by the month of February they held about 50 per cent of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, especially in the central part of that territory that they held, where the town of Malisevo is and the region of Drenica, the Drenica Mountains, the mountain of Milanovac. That's the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The document that we see right now on our screens in front of us, is this a document of yours?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document that I personally wrote to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell me, we see here a description of the roads, that some of them were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. For me as commander, the major problem was precisely that, the fact that roads from the territory of Metohija going to the territory of Kosovo, towards Pristina -- already in the months of January and February they were partly closed, and it was very risky to take these roads in individual vehicles, quite impossible in military vehicles. When convoys travelled down these roads, they had to have heavy security.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, would you please look at the eighth paragraph of this document. I think that it's on page 1 of the English too. It says: "The entire territory of Milanovac is under the control of the STS."

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you read it.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: "The entire territory of Mount Milanovac, which is bordered by the towns of Suva Reka, Orahovac, and Malisevo, is under the control of the Siptar terrorist forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: "According to our information as well (a reliable source), the territory between Prizren, Suva Reka, and Orahovac has recently also been taken almost entirely by the Siptar terrorist forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know roughly from when this document is?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the second page, please. Count 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at the second paragraph, in relation to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could the OSCE carry out -- or rather, did their activity have any effect on the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Although we expected that, obviously, judging by this large number of incidents, the OSCE could not have any effect on the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, these KLA activities, did they lead to the civilian population moving out?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: As far as the Serb and Montenegrin population is concerned, most of them moved out in 1998 already from those villages in my area where there were only a few houses respectively. So in 1999, the Serb population remained only in a few villages; that is, Velika Hoca, where only Serbs live, and the village of Novake, where only Serbs live. Then there were also Serbs in Smac, a few houses; in Zojic, a few houses; in Rastane, a few houses; and in Musutiste, which is a big village, it has a population of over 2.500. Half of the population were Serbs and the other half were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did both Serbs and Albanians move out?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: As far as Albanians are concerned, I know that in 1998 and 1999 people were moving out. In 1998, especially in the month of July, when this anti-terrorist action started. I had occasion several times on the ground to see that when the police would show up or when the army would show up, columns would be set up in villages consisting of tractors and other vehicles and that they would start leaving the villages concerned. Usually, the column would leave part of the village and move towards the army and the police and another part of the column, or a different column, would go in the opposite direction, if I can put it that way, towards the woods, towards the mountains. Often, especially this other part of the column, we could see that directly even with the naked eye, and sometimes we used binoculars as well. Sometimes they were followed by these forces of the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army, the UCK, that is. As the OSCE came in, the population returned to their villages within my area of responsibility, but I know that within the area of the Drenica mountains, that is, the part of Kosovo and Metohija where Malisevo is in the centre, I know that during the OSCE mission and up until the beginning of the aggression part of the population was outside their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. As far as villages are concerned, what was the basic principle of the KLA or UCK in relation to villages?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and in 1999, very often terrorists attacked from the villages themselves, because roads went through villages. However, what would happen would be that sometimes the civilian population was not in the village itself. They had been moved to another village beforehand. Or if this attack would take place, say, against smaller units of the police -- in most cases it happened to the police, attacks at individual patrols. When there would be intervention by stronger forces, when they would come to the aid of the attacked units, one could see that the terrorists were using the population as a human shield, although they believed and said that they were actually helping their population go to some other areas, deeper into the mountains or into the woods. There is also the term of "two villages" that is -- that exists in military practices. I saw that in 1998 and 1999 as well. One village would be in-depth as a logistics base, and the previous village that had been emptied, so to speak, at a given point in time terrorist forces appear there. They set up an ambush. They attack the military or the police from these ambushes, causing losses in their ranks, and then they would withdraw to the village that was their logistics base. Then again they could change back into civilian clothes, and from there they can either go to other safer areas or simply stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We are now going to move on to the beginning of the war. Could you please tell me -- actually, it's better if we have the map on our screens before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 32, please. 5D1332, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is this your map?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my work map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I chose this one because, frankly, its quality is the best in e-court. I'm going to ask you to explain and indicate on the map what area of defence you took up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, please. Zoom out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would you like it to be zoomed out now, or do you think it's right now?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
